name: Dice Rolls
content:
There are five main kinds of dice rolls in Renaissance: skill checks, luck checks, engagement rolls and damage rolls. The most common are skill checks:

SKILL CHECKS

When a character decides to take action and the outcome is uncertain, they make a SKILL CHECK.

To make a skill check, roll one fate die (d12) and a number of additional success dice (d6) determined by the character’s ranks in a given skill (see the Core Stats section). Add together all the dice to determine the result:

= 15

The result is then compared against an opposing roll, a static target, or is interpreted subjectively by the GM. Each of those three cases are considered a skill check, but each represents a different kind of skill check:

CONTESTS

If a character's action is actively opposed by another character or creature, it is a CONTEST. The character and their opponent each roll a skill check of their own, as above, and the two results are compared to determine the winner. On a tie, both sides re-roll.

Many character abilities call for contests, specifying which skills should be rolled. If the GM calls for an contest, they determine which skills each side must roll.

If there is no active opponent to the character's action, the result of the skill check is compared against a difficulty:

SKILL CHECKS AGAINST DIFFICULTY

If a character’s action isn’t contested but must overcome environmental challenges or demonstrate competence in a skill, the GM sets a DIFFICULTY for the skill check before the roll is made. In other cases, a character's ability may call for a skill check to be made against an opponent's stat or some other static number, in which case that stat or other number is the difficulty for the check.

Either way, if the result meets or exceeds the difficulty, the check passes: the character does what they set out to do. Otherwise, it is a failure. Use the scale below as a guide when setting difficulty:

If an action doesn't have a clear pass/fail outcome, the GM can choose to omit a difficulty and instead evaluate the roll result subjectively:

SUBJECTIVE SKILL CHECKS

Gathering information, observing your surroundings, social interaction - in situations like these, often the skill check is not determining whether an action is effective, but how effective it is. In these cases, the GM may simply see what the roll result is and react accordingly.

FAVORED & ILL-FAVORED

Various effects may call for a skill check to be FAVORED or ILL-FAVORED:

  • If a skill check is favored, roll the fate die twice and keep the higher result.

  • If a skill check is ill-favored, roll the fate die twice and keep the lower result.

Either way, you only roll the success dice (if any) once and add them to the fate die result to get the overall result:

FAVORED result would be 15 (10+5), ILL-FAVORED result would be 9 (4+5).

Favored and ill-favored cancel each other out. If a roll is already favored and an effect would make it ill-favored, it becomes a flat roll - just roll the fate die once. Similarly, if a roll is already ill-favored and an effect would make it favored, it becomes a flat roll.

Any number of these effects can stack, with each moving the roll toward favored or ill-favored. For example, if a roll is subject to one effect that makes it ill-favored and two effects that each make it favored, the net result would be a favored roll.

DICE BONUSES & PENALTIES

Various effects may add or remove success dice from the pool for a skill check. Throughout the game rules, you'll see this expressed in a shorthand. For example, "+1d" means "add one success die" to the skill check, "-2d" means "remove two success dice" from the skill check, and so on.

The maximum number of success dice for a skill check is 5. Taking +1d to a skill check that already includes 5 success dice makes the roll favored. Additional +d bonuses beyond that have no further effect.

The minimum number of success dice for a skill check is 0. Taking -1d to a skill check that already includes 0 success dice makes the roll ill-favored. Additional -d penalties beyond that have no further effect.

DICE RESULTS

When determining the result of a skill check, there are special rules for both types of dice:

FATE DIE (d12)

  • Rolling 1-10 on a fate die simply adds that number to the Check’s total result.

  • Rolling 12 on a fate die is Sol 🌞 - the best result:

    • The fate die adds 12 to the total roll result.

    • If you are in the Quest phase, the party moves one notch closer to Boon (see the Quest Mechanics section).

  • Rolling 11 on a fate die is Morte 💀 - the worst result:

    • The fate die adds 0 to the total roll result.

    • If you are in the Quest phase, the party moves one notch closer to Bane (see Per-Quest Mechanics) and the GM takes a Soft Move.

When determining whether one fate die roll is higher than another, Morte 💀 is considered 0, not 11.

Note that Sol 🌞 and Morte 💀 do not automatically dictate the outcome of the check. It is possible to fail/lose a skill check with a result that includes Sol 🌞, and it is possible to pass/win a skill check with a result that includes Morte 💀. The outcome of the check is still determined by comparing the overall roll result against a difficulty or an opponent's roll result.

SUCCESS DICE (d6)

  • Rolling 1-5 on a success die simply adds that number to the total roll result.

  • Rolling 6✨ adds that number to the total roll result AND gives you a success, which you can spend on various additional effects. Multiple 6✨s on a single roll means you have multiple successes to spend:

SPENDING SUCCESSES

If a skill check produces one or more SUCCESSES, regardless of the outcome of the check itself, you may spend each success to achieve one additional effect of your choice. Many abilities offer specific effects you can purchase with successes when using that ability, but these effects are always available to you:

  • Gain Insight. You discover a secret, a weakness, a resource, or some other useful detail, as determined by the GM.

  • Go Quietly. Your action is done quietly or without attracting attention, as determined by the GM.

  • Make Haste. Your action takes less time than expected, as determined by the GM.

  • Widen Influence. Your action affects more subjects than you originally aimed to affect, or the scale of the action's effects is broadened, as determined by the GM.

  • Take Advantage. Your action produces information or an effect that you and your allies can use to your advantage. You or an ally you choose takes +1d to their next skill check that is relevant to this skill check, as determined by the GM.

You may choose each effect multiple times for a given skill check. Unspent successes are forfeited after the skill check is resolved.

When resolving these effects, the player and GM should work together to make the outcome fit into the narrative of the game while giving the player a meaningful benefit, even if the overall roll result was a failure.

Another way to spend successes is to upgrade a failure to a pass/win with consequence:

PASS/WIN WITH CONSEQUENCE

If the result of a skill check is a failure/loss but includes one or more successes, the player may request (or the GM may offer) a PASS WITH CONSEQUENCE (against difficulty) or WIN WITH CONSEQUENCE (contest).

If the player and GM both accept, all of the successes are considered spent, the skill check is upgraded to a pass/win, and the GM takes a Soft Move (see the Phases of Play section).

The severity of the Soft Move should be commensurate with how far below the difficulty or opponent's result the check’s total result is. In extreme cases, the GM may even insist that a Hard Move would be necessary for pass/win with consequence.

Players are encouraged to keep their requests for pass/win with consequence reasonable and to reserve them for narratively significant moments in the game. The GM is generally encouraged to accept reasonable requests for a pass/win with consequence, but they have full discretion.

GROUP SKILL CHECK

When two or more characters attempt to overcome an obstacle as a group, the GM may call for a GROUP SKILL CHECK.

The GM sets a single difficulty and all participants roll skill checks against that difficulty to determine the outcome. The skill checks may all use the same skill or may vary, depending on the obstacle and how each character is contributing to the effort. The GM has discretion to accept or reject particular skills as relevant.

A majority of passes means the group skill check passes. A majority of failures means the group skill check fails. If there is a tie, the player who rolled the lowest result has the dubious honor of rolling a luck check (see Luck Checks below) as a tiebreaker.

Any successes rolled as part of a group skill check are still individual to the character that rolled them - they are the only one who can spend the successes.

However, on a group failure, if the total number of successes rolled by all participants is equal to or greater than the number of participants involved, the group may request (or the GM may offer) a pass with consequence, as defined above.

LUCK CHECKS

At their discretion, the GM may call for a LUCK CHECK to determine a variety of random factors throughout gameplay that are not dependent on characters' actions.

To make a luck check, a player simply rolls one fate die. In general, a roll of 1-5 or Morte 💀 results in bad luck, while a roll of 6-10 or Sol 🌞 results in good luck. The GM may also choose to define other thresholds for specific outcomes.

Note that players should always be the ones rolling the luck check, and rolling Morte 💀 or Sol 🌞 on a luck check does move the Quest toward Bane/Boon (see the Quest Mechanics section), as with a skill check. In the case of Morte 💀 - the GM also takes a Soft Move, as with a skill check.

Luck Checks should never be used to replace character skills or abilities. They should be used to determine truly random environmental factors: Does this barn happen to have a scythe in it that could be used as an improvised weapon? Does the blacksmith happen to be home at the moment? Was the mayor already assassinated before you opened the door?

ENGAGEMENT ROLLS

When two combatants engage in melee combat, there is a special step before each attack is resolved called ENGAGEMENT. In this step, each combatant rolls a variable number of dice to attempt to gain an advantage in the exchange. The interactions of the dice represent the maneuvers and footwork in hand-to-hand combat that precede an attempt to land a blow.

The rules of engagement are fully explained in the Combat section.

DAMAGE ROLLS

Various weapons, abilities, and effects call for DAMAGE ROLLS to help determine their impact. Damage rolls are made with varying sets of dice, determined by the weapon, ability, or effect that calls for the roll, and may include one or more dice of any type.

Similar to skill checks, damage rolls can be subject to bonuses and penalties, again represented by the same shorthand: +1d, +2d, -1d, -2d, etc. In the case, this means adding or removing damage dice from the dice pool for the damage roll.

Bonuses can increase the dice pool for a damage roll to any size, and penalties can reduce the dice pool to 0 dice (but not negative dice).

Some abilities upgrade or downgrade damage dice by one or more steps. The chain is:

d2 ↔ d4 ↔ d6 ↔ d8 ↔ d10 ↔ d12 ↔ d20

A damage die cannot be downgraded below d2 or upgraded above d20.

In general, you will add a modifier to the result of a damage roll. Typically the modifier will be one of your core stat scores (see the Core Stats section). If penalties reduce the dice pool for a damage roll to 0 dice, you still add together any modifiers to determine the result.

By default, the result of a damage roll determines the amount of Endurance the target loses (see the Core Stats section).
